question: What is the absolute ceiling?

options.text: The highest altitude approved for the type in the flight manual
The altitude where the rate of climb with all engines at maximum continuous power falls to zero
The altitude where the rate of climb falls to 300 ft/min
The altitude where low- and high-speed buffet coincide

explanation: At the absolute ceiling the theoretical rate of climb, with all engines at maximum continuous power, is zero. The service ceiling is lower, where a small specified rate of climb is still available.

question: What is the service ceiling?

options.text: The highest altitude at which the cabin can still be pressurised
The altitude that gives a 0.3 g margin to buffet
Where the rate of climb falls to a set small value
The altitude at which the rate of climb becomes zero

explanation: The service ceiling is where the rate of climb has dropped to a specified minimum value, so the aeroplane can still climb slowly. The absolute ceiling is where it drops to zero.

question: What is the aerodynamic ceiling?

options.text: The altitude where the rate of climb becomes zero
The altitude that gives a 0.3 g margin to both of the buffets
The altitude where maximum cruise thrust is reached
The altitude where the low-speed and high-speed buffet Mach numbers coincide in 1 g flight

explanation: At the aerodynamic ceiling, in unaccelerated 1 g level flight, the low-speed and high-speed buffet Mach numbers meet, leaving no speed margin at all.

question: What is the manoeuvre ceiling?

options.text: The pressure altitude giving a 0.3 g margin to both low- and high-speed buffet
The altitude where the two buffet Mach numbers coincide at 1 g
The altitude where the rate of climb is 300 ft/min
The altitude where a 60° bank turn is still possible

explanation: The manoeuvre (1.3 g) ceiling leaves a 0.3 g margin before buffet at either end of the speed range, so the aeroplane can manoeuvre or meet gusts without buffeting.

question: How is the altitude shown on performance charts normally defined?

options.text: As height above the aerodrome, read with QFE set
As density altitude, read from a slide rule
As pressure altitude, read with 1013 hPa set
As elevation above mean sea level, read with QNH set

explanation: Chart altitude is pressure altitude: the height in the standard atmosphere at which the prevailing pressure occurs, read with 1013 hPa on the subscale.

question: What is density altitude?

options.text: The height of the aerodrome above mean sea level
The ISA altitude with the same density
The altitude corrected for wind
The altitude in the standard atmosphere where the prevailing pressure is found

explanation: Density altitude is the ISA altitude that has the same air density as the actual conditions. Pressure altitude does the same for pressure only.

question: How is aerodrome elevation defined?

options.text: The elevation of the highest point of the landing area
The average elevation of all the runways
The elevation of the aerodrome reference point
The elevation of the lowest runway threshold

explanation: Aerodrome elevation is the elevation of the highest point of the landing area.

question: What does flight level 250 represent?

options.text: A height of 25 000 ft above the aerodrome
A density altitude of 25 000 ft
An altitude of 25 000 ft with QNH set
A pressure altitude of 25 000 ft

explanation: A flight level is a surface of constant pressure related to 1013.25 hPa, given in hundreds of feet of pressure altitude, so FL250 is 25 000 ft pressure altitude.

question: In performance terms, what is "height"?

options.text: The altitude read with 1013 hPa set
The distance from the cockpit to the ground
From the aeroplane's lowest part to a datum
The vertical distance from the aeroplane's CG down to mean sea level

explanation: Height is measured from the lowest part of the aeroplane to the relevant datum, which matters for screen heights and obstacle clearance.

question: What are the sea-level values of the international standard atmosphere?

options.text: 20°C, 1013.25 hPa and a density of 1.225 kg/m³
15°C, 1013.25 hPa and a density of 1.225 kg/m³
15°C, 1013.25 hPa and a density of 1.293 kg/m³
0°C, 1000 hPa and a density of 1.0 kg/m³

explanation: ISA sea level is 15°C, 1013.25 hPa (29.92 inHg) and 1.225 kg/m³, with dry air treated as a perfect gas.

question: What is the ISA temperature lapse rate up to the altitude where the temperature reaches −56.5°C?

options.text: 1.98°C per 1 000 ft
1.5°C per 1 000 ft
2.5°C per 1 000 ft
3.00°C per 1 000 ft

explanation: The ISA lapse rate is 0.65°C per 100 m, or 1.98°C (about 2°C) per 1 000 ft, up to −56.5°C.

question: What is the take-off run available (TORA)?

options.text: The runway length plus any clearway
The runway length plus any stopway
The length from the threshold to the first obstacle beyond it
The declared length usable for the ground run

explanation: TORA runs from where the take-off run can begin to the nearest point where the surface can no longer bear the aeroplane's weight in normal operation; usually threshold to threshold.

question: How is the accelerate-stop distance available (ASDA) made up?

options.text: TODA plus any stopway
TORA plus any clearway
TORA plus half the clearway
TORA plus any stopway

explanation: ASDA = TORA + stopway. It is the distance in which the aeroplane can be brought to rest in an emergency without risk of accident.

question: How is the take-off distance available (TODA) made up?

options.text: TORA plus stopway, but not more than 1.5 × TORA
TORA plus clearway, up to 1.5 × TORA
TORA plus stopway plus clearway
TORA plus clearway, with no limit

explanation: TODA = TORA + clearway, but the clearway counted may not exceed half the TORA, so TODA can never exceed 1.5 × TORA.

question: A runway has a TORA of 2 400 m and a clearway of 1 500 m. What TODA can be used?
explanation: Only half the TORA (1 200 m) of clearway can be counted, so TODA = 2 400 + 1 200 = 3 600 m, not 3 900 m.

question: When is a runway described as having a balanced field?

options.text: When ASDA equals TODA
When the runway has no slope
When the stopway equals the clearway in length
When TORA equals ASDA

explanation: A balanced field has an accelerate-stop distance available equal to the take-off distance available. A runway with neither stopway nor clearway is balanced.

question: What is the minimum width of a clearway?

options.text: The width of the runway

explanation: A clearway is at least 152 m (500 ft) wide, centred on the extended centre line and under the control of the airport authority.

question: What is the maximum upward slope of the clearway plane?
explanation: The clearway plane rises from the runway end at no more than 1.25%, and no object or terrain may protrude above it.

question: Which objects may protrude above the clearway plane?

options.text: Approach lights on the extended centre line up to 1 m high
Side threshold lights up to 0.66 m high
Nothing at all, without exception
Any frangible object up to 2 m high

explanation: Threshold lights may protrude if they are 0.66 m (26 in) or less above the runway end and are located to each side of the runway.

question: What is a stopway?

options.text: An area beyond the runway that can support a rejected take-off
The area beside the runway used to protect aircraft running off it
The paved area before the threshold used for taxiing
An obstacle-free area beyond the runway used for the airborne part of the take-off

explanation: A stopway is at least as wide as the runway, centred on it, able to support the aeroplane during an abandoned take-off without structural damage, and designated for decelerating.

question: What is the landing distance available (LDA)?

options.text: From where landing can begin to the end of the usable surface
The runway length plus any stopway
The distance from the threshold to the first taxiway exit on the runway
The full runway length from end to end

explanation: The LDA starts at the point above which the landing can begin, having regard to obstructions in the approach, and ends where the surface cannot bear the aeroplane or an obstacle affects safety.

question: What is the screen in performance terms?

options.text: A radar display used by the test pilots
A net at the end of the runway to stop aeroplanes that overrun
An imaginary barrier at TODA end or LDA start
The height at which the gear is retracted

explanation: The screen is imaginary, placed at the end of the TODA or the beginning of the LDA. Test pilots use its height when measuring take-off and landing performance.

question: When is a runway considered damp?

options.text: When it is reflective but has no standing water
When it has been raining in the last hour
When more than 25% is covered by water over 3 mm deep
When it is not dry but the moisture does not make it shiny

explanation: A damp runway is not dry, but its moisture does not give it a shiny appearance. A wet runway looks reflective.

question: When is a runway considered wet?

options.text: When more than 25% of it is covered with water over 3 mm deep
When reflective, with no significant standing water
When the braking coefficient is below 0.2
When it is not dry but not shiny

explanation: A wet runway is covered with enough water or moisture to look reflective, but without significant areas of standing water.

question: When is a runway considered contaminated by water?

options.text: When more than 50% of its area is covered by water more than 1 mm deep
When more than 10% is covered by water of any depth
When the surface is reflective
When over 25% has water deeper than 3 mm

explanation: A runway is contaminated when more than 25% of the surface area being used is covered by surface water more than 3 mm deep, or by slush or loose snow equivalent to more than 3 mm of water.

question: Which runway is classed as dry?

options.text: Any runway that is damp but not wet
Any runway with no standing water on its surface at all
One neither wet nor contaminated
Only an unpaved runway in summer

explanation: A dry runway is neither wet nor contaminated. It includes paved runways with grooves or porous pavement maintained to keep effectively dry braking even when moisture is present.

question: What is the aerodrome reference point?

options.text: The start of the main runway
The aerodrome's location and ATZ centre
The highest point on the landing area
The point at which the altimeters of departing aeroplanes are checked

explanation: The aerodrome reference point defines the aerodrome's location and is the centre of its traffic zone where one is established.

question: How should an aeroplane's classification number be compared with a pavement's classification number?

options.text: The aeroplane's number must not exceed the pavement's
The two numbers are unrelated to operations
The pavement's number must not exceed the aeroplane's
The aeroplane's number must be at least twice the pavement's number

explanation: The aircraft's classification number shows its load effect on a pavement; normal operation is allowed when it does not exceed the pavement's classification number. Newer systems use rating rather than classification numbers in the same way.

question: What is calibrated airspeed (CAS)?

options.text: True airspeed corrected for wind
IAS corrected for position and instrument error
Equivalent airspeed corrected for density
Indicated airspeed corrected for compressibility error

explanation: CAS is IAS corrected for position and instrument errors. In the standard atmosphere at mean sea level it equals TAS.

question: What is equivalent airspeed (EAS)?

options.text: True airspeed corrected for temperature
Calibrated airspeed corrected for density
Calibrated airspeed corrected for compressibility
Indicated airspeed corrected for position error

explanation: EAS is CAS corrected for compressibility at the pressure altitude concerned. Correcting EAS for density gives TAS.

question: What is indicated airspeed?

options.text: The uncorrected airspeed indicator reading
The speed relative to the undisturbed air
The speed over the ground
The airspeed corrected for instrument error only

explanation: IAS is shown by the pitot-static airspeed indicator, calibrated for standard sea-level compressible flow but uncorrected for airspeed system errors.

question: What is Mach number?

options.text: True airspeed minus the local speed of sound
The ratio of indicated airspeed to the speed of sound at sea level
The ratio of ground speed to true airspeed
The ratio of true airspeed to the local speed of sound

explanation: Mach number = TAS ÷ local speed of sound.

question: What is the air minimum control speed, VMCA?

options.text: The lowest speed for control with all engines at idle
The lowest speed at which the aeroplane can lift off
The lowest airborne control speed with the critical engine out
The lowest speed for directional control on the ground after an engine failure

explanation: VMCA is the minimum speed at which directional control can be maintained in the air with the critical engine inoperative and the others at take-off thrust.

question: How much bank may be used when VMCA is established?

options.text: None; wings must be level
No more than 5°, towards the inoperative engine
No more than 15°, towards the inoperative engine
Up to 5°, away from the dead engine

explanation: Full opposite rudder and not more than 5° of bank away from the inoperative engine (towards the live engine) are allowed when establishing VMCA.

question: What is the maximum value VMCA may have relative to the stall speed?

options.text: 1.13 VSR (or 1.2 VS1)
1.05 VSR (or 1.1 VS1)
1.3 VSR (or 1.4 VS1)
1.23 VSR (or 1.3 VS1)

explanation: VMCA may not exceed 1.13 VSR, or 1.2 VS1, so that it stays below the speeds at which the aeroplane must be flown after take-off.

question: When the ground minimum control speed, VMCG, is established, which control may NOT be used?

options.text: Primary flight controls
Nose-wheel steering
Rudder
Forward elevator pressure on the nose wheel

explanation: VMCG is demonstrated using only the primary flight controls. Forward elevator pressure to keep the nose wheel down is allowed; nose-wheel steering and throttling the opposite engine are not.

question: What is the landing minimum control speed, VMCL?

options.text: The lowest speed at which reverse thrust can be used
The reference speed at 50 ft above the threshold
The lowest approach speed for control if the critical engine fails
The lowest speed at which the aeroplane can touch down on the runway

explanation: VMCL is the minimum speed on the approach at which, if the critical engine suddenly fails, control can be maintained, and thrust can be moved between idle and maximum without dangerous characteristics.

question: What is the critical engine?

options.text: The engine with the highest hours since its last overhaul
The engine whose failure is worst for performance or handling
The engine nearest the fuselage
The engine that drives the main hydraulic pump

explanation: The critical engine is the one whose failure would have the worst effect on the aeroplane's performance or handling.

question: What is VEF?

options.text: The speed at which the pilot recognises the engine failure
The highest speed at which the take-off can be rejected
The minimum speed for take-off with one engine inoperative
The CAS at which the critical engine is assumed to fail

explanation: VEF is the CAS at which the critical engine is assumed to fail for performance calculations. It is never less than VMCG.

question: Which speed may VEF never be less than?

options.text: VMCG
V1
VMCA
VR

explanation: An engine failure below VMCG would leave the aeroplane uncontrollable on the ground, so VEF is never less than VMCG.

question: Which statement describes V1?

options.text: The speed at which the aeroplane lifts off the runway
The minimum speed for directional control on the ground
The speed reached at the screen height with one engine inoperative
The highest speed for the first stopping action within ASD

explanation: V1 is the maximum speed at which the pilot can take the first action to stop within the accelerate-stop distance, and also the minimum speed from which, after an engine failure at VEF, the take-off can be continued within the take-off distance.

question: An engine fails before V1. What should the pilot do?

options.text: Reject only if the runway is dry
Reject the take-off
Continue if the speed is above VMCG
Continue the take-off

explanation: Before V1 there is not enough distance to continue safely with one engine inoperative, so the take-off is rejected. At or above V1 it is continued.

question: What is the minimum unstick speed, VMU?

options.text: The lowest demonstrated speed for a safe lift-off
The speed at which rotation is started
The speed at which the nose wheel leaves the runway
The minimum speed for directional control after the lift-off

explanation: VMU is the lowest speed, for each weight, thrust and configuration, at which a safe take-off has been demonstrated.

question: What is the take-off safety speed?

options.text: The speed for best rate of climb with all engines
The minimum speed for directional control on the ground
A speed after lift-off giving the required OEI climb
The speed at which the take-off must be rejected

explanation: The take-off safety speed is reached after lift-off and gives the required one-engine-inoperative climb performance. For Class A aeroplanes it is V2.

question: What is the reference landing speed, VREF?

options.text: The speed at touchdown
The landing screen speed used for distances
The lowest speed for control with an engine failed on the approach
The speed for maximum glide range

explanation: VREF is the speed, in a specified landing configuration, at which the aeroplane descends through the landing screen height in the determination of landing distance.

question: What does VMBE mean?

options.text: The minimum speed at which the wheel brakes become effective
The maximum speed for nose-wheel steering
The maximum speed for using reverse thrust
The highest speed the brakes can safely stop from

explanation: VMBE is the maximum brake energy speed: above it, the brakes cannot absorb the energy needed to stop safely.

question: What is VZF?

options.text: The minimum safe speed with zero flap
The maximum speed with flaps extended
The speed at which the flap retraction must be started
The stall speed with zero flap

explanation: VZF, the zero flap speed, is the minimum safe manoeuvring speed with flaps retracted.

question: What is the difference between VLO and VLE?

options.text: They are always identical
VLO is with the gear extended; VLE is for extending it
VLO: moving the gear; VLE: gear down
VLO applies to flaps, VLE to the gear

explanation: VLO is the maximum speed at which the gear may be safely extended or retracted; VLE is the maximum speed at which the aeroplane may be flown with the gear extended.

question: What is VFE?

options.text: The speed at which the critical engine fails
The highest speed with flaps at a given setting
The final take-off speed
The speed at which the flaps should normally be extended

explanation: VFE is the flap extended speed: the highest speed permitted with the flaps in a prescribed extended position.

question: What is VX?

options.text: The speed for the best rate of climb
The speed for minimum drag
The design manoeuvring speed
The best angle of climb speed

explanation: VX gives the steepest climb gradient; VY gives the greatest rate of climb.

question: What is VGO?

options.text: The lowest decision speed for an OEI take-off in TODA
The speed at which the aeroplane must be rotated
The speed at which go-around thrust is set
The highest decision speed from which the aeroplane can stop within ASDA

explanation: VGO is the lowest decision speed for a continued take-off within TODA; VSTOP is the highest decision speed for a stop within ASDA. V1 must lie between them.

question: What is VSTOP?

options.text: The speed at which reverse thrust is cancelled
The speed at which the brakes overheat
The highest decision speed from which the aeroplane can stop within ASDA
The lowest speed from which the take-off can be continued safely

explanation: VSTOP is the highest decision speed for stopping within the accelerate-stop distance available.

question: What is VS0?

options.text: The stall speed with zero flap
The one-g stall speed at maximum mass
The stall speed in the landing configuration
The stall speed in the take-off configuration with gear down

explanation: VS0 is the stall speed in the landing configuration. VS1 is the stall speed in the configuration under consideration.

question: What is VSR?

options.text: The speed at which the stick shaker first activates
The reference stall speed (1 g stall)
The stall speed with landing flap only
The stall speed in a 30° bank

explanation: VSR is the reference stall speed and is assumed to be the same as VS1g, the speed at which the wing can still make lift equal to weight. VSR0 is in the landing configuration.

question: What is the final take-off speed, VFTO?

options.text: The OEI speed at the end of the take-off path
The speed at which the gear is retracted
The best rate of climb speed with all engines operating
The speed at the screen height

explanation: VFTO is the one-engine-inoperative speed at the end of the take-off flight path in the en route configuration; it is also the final segment speed.

question: What do V3 and V4 refer to?

options.text: The landing and go-around speeds
The flap retraction speeds for flap 3 and flap 4
One-engine-inoperative climb speeds in segments 3 and 4
All-engines initial and take-off climb speeds

explanation: V3 is the all-engines-operating steady initial climb speed; V4 is the all-engines-operating steady take-off climb speed.

question: What do VMD and VMP stand for?

options.text: Minimum dive speed and maximum propeller speed
Minimum descent speed and minimum pitch speed
Minimum drag speed and minimum power speed
Maximum dive speed and maximum power speed

explanation: VMD is the speed for minimum drag; VMP is the speed for minimum power required, which is slower than VMD.

question: Which speed replaced the older "VAT" landing speed?

options.text: VFTO
V2
VZF
VREF

explanation: VREF, the reference landing speed, replaced the older VAT speed.

question: What is VRA?

options.text: The rotation speed with anti-ice on
The rough air (turbulence) speed
The reverse thrust cancel speed
The design manoeuvring speed

explanation: VRA is the turbulence or rough air speed. VA is the design manoeuvring speed.

question: What is a baulked landing?

options.text: An unexpectedly discontinued landing
A landing beyond the touchdown zone
A landing made with one engine inoperative
A landing on a contaminated runway

explanation: A baulked landing is a landing manoeuvre that is discontinued unexpectedly, after which the aeroplane climbs away.

question: What is brake horsepower?

options.text: The power lost in the propeller
The power at the main output shaft
The power used by the engine-driven pumps
The power absorbed by the wheel brakes when stopping

explanation: Brake horsepower is the power delivered at the main output shaft of the engine.

question: How is climb gradient expressed?

options.text: Vertical interval divided by distance flown through the air, in degrees
Rate of climb divided by indicated airspeed
Horizontal distance divided by height gained
Vertical interval divided by horizontal interval, as a percentage

explanation: Gradient = vertical interval ÷ horizontal interval × 100, with both in the same units.

question: An aeroplane climbs 600 ft while travelling 10 000 ft horizontally. What is its climb gradient?
explanation: 600 ÷ 10 000 × 100 = 6%. Dividing the other way round gives 16.7%.

question: What is specific fuel consumption (SFC) for a jet engine?

options.text: Fuel flow per unit of thrust
Fuel used per passenger mile
Fuel flow per hour
Distance flown per unit of fuel

explanation: SFC is fuel flow per unit of thrust; the lower it is, the more efficient the engine.

question: What is gross performance?

options.text: The average performance a fleet should achieve if well maintained and flown as described
The performance achieved by a new aeroplane flown by test pilots
The worst performance any aeroplane of the type has shown
The average performance reduced by a statistical safety margin

explanation: Gross performance is the fleet average for well-maintained aeroplanes flown with the manual's techniques. Measured performance is that of new aeroplanes flown by test pilots.

question: What is net performance?

options.text: Gross performance increased for a new aeroplane of the type
The measured performance from certification flights
The average performance with all engines operating
Gross performance reduced to allow for contingencies that cannot be accounted for operationally

explanation: Net performance is gross performance diminished to cover things like variations in piloting technique and temporary below-average performance. It is very unlikely not to be achieved.

question: What is measured performance?

options.text: The performance measured by the operator after each flight
The performance achieved by the manufacturer in certification tests
The average performance of a fleet in service
The performance after the safety margins are applied

explanation: Measured performance comes from new aeroplanes flown by test pilots for certification, so it is better than an average fleet will achieve.

question: About how likely is it that net performance will not be achieved?

options.text: About one chance in a hundred
About one chance in ten thousand
Less than one chance in a million
About one chance in a thousand

explanation: Net performance is set about five standard deviations below the gross (average) performance, so the chance of not achieving it is less than one in a million.

question: What is gross height in the take-off flight path?

options.text: The height reached using the net climb performance
The pressure altitude of the aerodrome
The height above the highest obstacle
The height from gross climb performance

explanation: Gross height uses gross climb performance. It is used for pressure altitudes for obstacle clearance and the height at which flap retraction begins.

question: What is net height in the take-off flight path used for?

options.text: To find the screen height for landing
To set the cabin altitude
To check obstacle clearance by the net path
To decide the height at which the flaps are retracted

explanation: Net height uses net climb performance, giving the net flight path that must clear all obstacles by the statutory margin.

question: For what time is take-off power or thrust normally limited?

options.text: 5 min, or 10 min after a failure if approved
2 minutes, or 5 minutes after an engine failure
10 minutes in all cases
15 minutes, or until 1 500 ft

explanation: Take-off power or thrust is limited to a continuous period of 5 minutes, or for turbine aeroplanes, when requested, 10 minutes after a power unit has failed.

question: For how long may maximum continuous thrust be used?

options.text: For 30 minutes at a time
For unrestricted periods
For 10 minutes
For 5 minutes

explanation: Maximum continuous thrust or power is the rating for periods of unrestricted duration.

question: What is continuous one-engine-inoperative thrust?

options.text: The thrust used for the take-off run only
Unrestricted thrust after an engine failure
The thrust needed to hold altitude at VMD
The thrust set during a rejected take-off

explanation: It is the thrust identified in the performance data for use after take-off when a power unit has failed or been shut down, for periods of unrestricted duration.

question: How is the en route phase defined for a Class B aeroplane?

options.text: From 1 500 ft above the take-off surface to 1 500 ft above the landing aerodrome
From 400 ft above the take-off surface to 1 000 ft above the landing aerodrome
From 1 500 ft above the take-off surface to 1 000 ft above the landing aerodrome
From the screen height to the top of descent

explanation: For Class B the en route phase runs from 1 500 ft above the take-off surface to 1 000 ft above the landing aerodrome; for Class A it ends at 1 500 ft above the landing aerodrome.

question: What is a large aeroplane?

options.text: One over 5 700 kg, not commuter category
Any multi-engine aeroplane
Any aeroplane with more than 19 passenger seats fitted
Any jet aeroplane

explanation: A large aeroplane has a maximum certificated take-off mass of more than 5 700 kg; the commuter category is not included.

question: What is load factor?

options.text: The ratio of traffic load to the maximum take-off mass
The ratio of lift to drag
The ratio of thrust to weight
The ratio of a specified load to weight

explanation: Load factor is the ratio of a specified load (aerodynamic, inertia or ground reaction) to the aeroplane's weight; in level flight it is 1 g.

question: Motion about which axis is yaw?

options.text: The lateral axis
The propeller axis
The normal (vertical) axis
The longitudinal axis

explanation: Yaw is about the normal axis, roll about the longitudinal axis and pitch about the lateral axis.

question: What is a frangible object?

options.text: One that breaks or yields if struck
One made only of plastic or rubber
One that can be removed quickly from the runway strip
One that is painted in high-visibility colours

explanation: A frangible object retains its integrity up to a specified load but breaks, distorts or yields under greater load or impact so as to present minimum hazard to an aircraft.

question: What is windshear?

options.text: A steady crosswind over the whole runway
Turbulence caused only by mountains
The wind gradient above 1 000 ft
A local change in wind speed or direction over a short distance

explanation: Windshear is a localised change of wind speed and/or direction over a short distance, which can cause sudden airspeed changes, dangerous near take-off and landing.

question: In performance abbreviations, what does N−1 mean?

options.text: Fan speed reduced by 1%
One engine inoperative
All engines operating
One engine at idle

explanation: N means all engines operating; N−1 one engine inoperative; N−2 two engines inoperative. N1 is the fan rotation speed.

question: What does the abbreviation WAT stand for?

options.text: Weight–altitude–temperature
Wind–altitude–track
Weight at take-off
Wet and treated runway

explanation: WAT (or MAT, mass–altitude–temperature) refers to the climb-limited mass, which depends on weight, altitude and temperature.

question: What does EMDA mean?

options.text: Emergency descent altitude
Extended minimum drag airspeed
Emergency distance available, the same as ASDA
Engine maximum demonstrated altitude

explanation: EMDA is the emergency distance available, another name for the accelerate-stop distance available.

question: What does "RZ" stand for in performance?

options.text: Runway zone
Rotation zero
Rate zero
Reference zero

explanation: Reference zero is the point on the ground or clearway plane below the screen at the end of the take-off distance required, from which the take-off flight path is measured.

question: Which aeroplanes are in performance Class A?

options.text: Propeller aeroplanes with 9 seats or less and 5 700 kg or less
All multi-engine jets, and multi-engine turboprops with more than 9 seats or over 5 700 kg
All aeroplanes over 5 700 kg, whatever the engines
Piston aeroplanes with more than 9 seats or over 5 700 kg

explanation: Class A covers all multi-engine turbojets and multi-engine turboprops with more than 9 passenger seats or a maximum take-off mass above 5 700 kg. They are certified to the large aeroplane code.

question: Which aeroplanes are in performance Class B?

options.text: All single-engine aeroplanes of any mass
Propeller aeroplanes with 9 passenger seats or less and 5 700 kg or less
Jet aeroplanes with 9 passenger seats or less
Propeller aeroplanes with more than 9 seats

explanation: Class B is propeller aeroplanes with a maximum approved passenger seating of 9 or less and a maximum take-off mass of 5 700 kg or less, certified to the small aeroplane code.

question: Which aeroplanes are in performance Class C?

options.text: Piston-engine aeroplanes with more than 9 seats or over 5 700 kg
All aeroplanes with 9 seats or less
Seaplanes and supersonic aeroplanes
Turboprop aeroplanes with more than 9 seats

question: Which aeroplanes are "unclassified" for performance?

options.text: Those older than 30 years
Those with no flight manual
Those with unique characteristics, such as supersonic aeroplanes and seaplanes
Those used only for private flying

explanation: Unclassified aeroplanes need special performance consideration, such as supersonic aeroplanes and seaplanes.

question: A twin turboprop has 9 passenger seats and a maximum take-off mass of 5 200 kg. Which performance class is it?

options.text: Class C
Unclassified
Class A
Class B

explanation: With 9 seats or less and 5 700 kg or less, a propeller aeroplane is Class B. Over either limit, a turboprop twin would be Class A.

question: A twin-engine business jet has 8 passenger seats and a maximum take-off mass of 4 900 kg. Which performance class is it?

options.text: Unclassified
Class C
Class B
Class A

explanation: All multi-engine turbojets are Class A, whatever their mass or seating. Class B applies only to propeller aeroplanes.

question: A twin piston aeroplane has 12 passenger seats and a maximum take-off mass of 6 200 kg. Which performance class is it?

options.text: Class B
Class A
Class C
Unclassified

explanation: Reciprocating-engine aeroplanes with more than 9 seats or above 5 700 kg are Class C.
